beta_new: The standard route leaves the trail system at Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) on the Devore Creek Trail and goes cross-country: through open forest and meadow to a saddle just south of Enigma Peak (~6,400 ft), down a scree gully to cross upper Castle Creek, then up Flora's southwest ridge on talus and scree to the summit. It is rated the least difficult of the Stehekin-area 'Top 100' peaks (compare neighboring Devore, Tupshin, and Riddle) and requires no rope, rack, or technical rock climbing — just sturdy boots, off-trail navigation, and tolerance for loose rock. The peak's namesake first ascent (Leuthold/Metzger, 1940) is attested for the mountain overall, but no published account gives it used this specific southwest line, so it is not attributed to the route here.

moves.value: A longer alternate approach reaches the same southwest slope and west cirque from Holden Village via Railroad Creek Road and Tenmile Pass; it is used mainly by parties combining Flora with Riddle Peak and Black Tower.
moves.from: An alternate, longer approach reaches the same southwest slope/west cirque from Holden Village via Railroad Creek Road and Tenmile Pass, used mainly by parties combining Flora with Riddle Peak and Black Tower.

beta_new: Ten pitches of varied terrain: straightforward gear climbing low down, a full-rope-length rightward traverse, easy walking/scrambling sections, awkward corner moves, hand-crack options, a sustained pitch, exposed traverses (with an optional wide-crack variant), and an easy finish to the summit plateau.

From the East Ridge saddle beside the Solitary Gendarme, downclimb the dirty gully on the north side for roughly 100 ft and exit left (northwest) onto the ledges - going lower runs into cliffs. Traverse northwest across roughly five rock ribs on sandy, grassy ledges and down-sloping slabs, mostly 3rd class with short 4th-class moves at each rib, staying close to the level at which the gully was left: too low meets the cliffs above the Boston Glacier, too high the steeper, corrugated ribs. Cairns mark the easiest line across most rib crossings (a higher and lower cairn at each rib). Where the North Ridge stops the traverse, climb the small northeast face below the summit: 3rd-class ledges, a short grassy traverse west to the next rib, then steepening Class 4 to the summit rocks. The face is lined with slung rappel stations that can double as belays; many parties belay the upper part. Allow about 2 hours from the saddle to the summit, more if belaying.

value.text: A single 50-60 m rope, a few small cams and nuts, and runners.

moves.from: Carry a single 50-60 m rope, a few small cams and nuts, and runners.

beta_new: From a notch on the East Ridge, climb the crest and both flanks of the ridge for 6-8 pitches, bypassing several gendarmes on ledges or short rappels into notches; the crux is a well-protected ~40 ft 5.8 section on the last gendarme, followed by easier simul-climbing to the summit.

Grade III, with the hardest ridge moves about 5.6. From Boston Basin high camp, cross the Quien Sabe Glacier to Sharkfin Col (a short 5.7 step and a class 3 gully), rappel to the Boston Glacier, and join the north ridge near 7,700 ft for an exposed run of moderate granite to the summit.

Also known as the "Chiwawa River route," this line is frequently combined with an ascent of neighboring Chiwawa Mountain from the same high camp at the ~7,200 ft col. Rock quality is notably better on the East Ridge itself than in the approach gully or on Fortress's southwest face.

Start at the Fortress-Chiwawa col. The rock band directly above is the only real climbing: a slabby move is the crux, then a chimney on the left breaks through. Above it a long snow slope steepens gradually toward the Southeast Ridge. Aim for the crest to the left of the point that looks like the summit, which is not the top, and follow the ridge to the high point. It is a mixed rock-and-snow route rather than a scramble, so bring a rope for the rock band.

Also referred to as the "Buck Creek route" or simply the standard/south ridge route. From the alpine basin below Pass No Pass, ascend green slopes and scree that steepen into class 2-3 talus and slab; the direct gully up the face is the loosest ground on the mountain, and many parties angle right onto slabbier rock or follow the south ridge crest instead. Reported ascent time from a high camp in the Pass No Pass basin is roughly 3.5-4 hours, with about 2.5-3 hours back down.

P1 (10+/11-, ~100 ft) climbs a nondescript crack to a two-piece fixed anchor on a pedestal. P2 (mid-11, ~82 ft) follows obvious double incipient cracks to a sweet final move and a series of ledges. P3 (10-, ~40 ft) is short with a tricky start then easy climbing. P4 (5.9, ~164 ft) climbs a beautiful right-facing corner. P5 and P6 (5.easy, ~262 ft and ~25 ft) trend right to join the South Arete and finish to the summit.

From Gardner Meadows (~10.5 mi in), leave the trail and ascend the grassy/brushy west side of the small stream draining south off Gardner Mountain, aiming for a small meadow basin around 6,200-7,100 ft. From there the route climbs a long, tedious slope of loose, marble-sized scree over sand (roughly 1,400 ft of gain in about half a mile) to reach the upper ridge/summit plateau, then finishes with a short, easier ridge scramble (some hand-holds, brief exposure) to the true summit. A faint climber's path exists on the scree in places but is easy to lose. Parties continuing to North Gardner Mountain descend west along the summit ridge to a false summit, then drop and scramble through loose rock/scree (and snow in early season) to a saddle near Point 8487, from which the ridge continues north over Point 8487 to North Gardner. Taken along the crest, the stretch between Gardner and Point 8487 is notably harder than the ascent of Gardner itself (class 3-4 around gendarmes and pinnacles; a lower line below the cliffs avoids the hardest of it), while the ridge from Point 8487 on to North Gardner stays mostly class 2.

Low-angle, runout slab climbing for the first ~12 pitches (soloable for confident 5.8 climbers early on), a very runout, fair-quality middle section (pitches 13-18, with 15-17 hard to protect), and a harder, well-bolted finish (pitches 19-23) with two 5.10 pitches.
Moderate trad climbing up to 5.9 with good protection on most pitches; the crux-adjacent middle slabs are serious (R/X-rated) with real rockfall/fall exposure.

The old sketch landmarks are still the way people navigate it: dirt gully, slab, canyon edge, tiny notch, razorback, glade saddle, key ledge traverse, Y notch, #2 gully. Walk up the dry creek bed from the road; partway up the route leaves the streambed into the woods on faint trail and flagging. At about 2,200 ft you reach the dirt gully — fill water at the creek here, it is the last certain water on the route. Four hundred vertical feet of loose dirt and rock, then the trail exits left into brush-free timber for another 400 ft, then the slab, which is two pitches of comfortable soloing on intersecting dikes. Above the slab continue in dirt along its upper left edge, traverse under a rock outcrop, over the razorback and tiny notch to the Glade Saddle, where there is a tight, well-used two-person bivy site. The wooded ramp above has a sporty 20-foot step. The Key Ledge Traverse is the most overstated part of the description — after the dirt gully it feels like a walk. It ends at the Y Notch, the confluence of #1 and #2 Gullies at the head of the Great Canyon. A short exposed step around a rock band, then several hundred yards of very steep brush and brush-tunnel on faint trail, brings you to the base of #2 Gully. The gully is a nightmarish mix of impossibly loose rock on one side and polished mossy rock on the other — do not attempt it unless bone dry. Simulclimb the lower section with short belayed steps, then pitch out the harder ground; a fixed ring piton partway up may date to the 1940 first ascent. The 'Chimney Variation' (two leads of easy class 5 above the chimney, a good idea if the chimney is wet) rejoins the standard line at the top of #2 Gully around 5,200 ft, from where easy slabs and steep heather lead to the summit.

value.name: Glade Saddle
value.notes: A tight, well-used two-person bivy site at the saddle above the razorback.

moves.from: Glade Saddle, where there is a tight, well-used two-person bivy site.

beta_new: Gato Negro is a full-day alpine rock climb with fairly sustained 5.10a/b climbing spread across 12 long pitches. Most pitches span 180-190 feet with none shorter than 150 feet. The route features a spectacular hand-crack first pitch, bolted 5.10a face climbing on fragile flakes, rising traverses under roofs, and splitter cracks on the final headwall. Route-finding is somewhat challenging; avoid a clean blocky chimney to the right of the route that looks good but is not as good as it appears. Cruxes are mostly well-protected, but a few slightly runout 5.8 sections on loose granite and a 5.9+ offwidth chimney section present additional challenges.

Ghost Peak is normally climbed as an add-on from a high camp shared with neighboring Crooked Thumb Peak and Phantom Peak, since all three summits are within a few tenths of a mile of one another in the Northern Pickets. The way from camp is obvious once you're established there. The first-ascent party climbed from the notch south of the peak, reaching it from the west, then kept to the south and west sides of the mountain along obvious weaknesses — easy-to-moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing on comparatively solid Pickets rock.

From the South Tieton Creek/Conrad Meadows trailhead, this route climbs the east side of Conrad Glacier to a saddle around 7,200 ft, then traverses onto Meade Glacier before a final push over boulders, scree, and a summit snowfield to the top. It is a summer and fall climb, not a spring or winter one, and is usually done car-to-car over two or more days.

Climb the glacier (now largely a series of persistent snowfields rather than a crevassed glacier) near the center of the cirque, right of the rock band that splits the upper and lower sections, then right of the snow dome to gain the ridge. A rough goat and boot path on the usually snow-free southwest side leads to a small saddle just east of the true summit, and a short, loose class 3 scramble finishes it. Popular and the most straightforward line up the peak, though it is a long outing (~20 miles round trip) with real elevation gain.

moves.from: From the Conrad Meadows / South Fork Tieton Trailhead, follow Trail #1120 through Conrad Meadows to the Surprise Lake loop and take its right fork to the trail's high point. Leave the trail there, climb west into a basin, pass between a pair of big mounds and drop briefly to the foot of the Meade Glacier.

beta_new: From Cispus Basin (reached from a camp in the timber below Snowgrass Flats, or camped in the basin itself, by following the PCT southbound), climbers go up to the saddle at the basin's northeast end and traverse a series of rock ribs and shallow gullies (the 'Goat Ledges' and 'Goat Ribs') at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft toward Gilbert Peak. The key navigational feature is a band of solid, abrasive white pyroclastic aggregate that points toward a notch behind a prominent dark rock tower nicknamed the 'black prow'; staying on this band (rather than the looser rock above or below it) is described as the safest line. A lower variation holds a consistent ~7,500 ft traverse elevation to reduce exposure to party-induced rockfall. The route is regarded by some as loose and dangerous, but careful route-finding along the white band and goat paths allows a safer Class 2-3 passage to the summit.

From a high camp near Glacier Ridge/Kennedy Glacier, climb the ridge on snow or loose rock with occasional protection to the top, where the 'Rabbit Ears' notch requires descending class 3 rock for about 150 feet to a saddle. From the saddle, climb an alpine ice face (roughly two pitches, up to ~60° in recent conditions, AI1-2 to AI2) to reach the crater rim and summit. Conditions vary significantly by year and season — early-season snow climbing has increasingly given way to exposed glacier ice even in June/July per recent trip reports.

From a camp near Glacier Creek, follow a climbers' trail up a gully to the top of Kennedy Ridge, then descend (right) to the foot of the Kennedy Glacier. Ascend the lower glacier keeping right, then the center of the upper glacier. Approach the bergschrund at the head of the glacier by ascending left to the top of a snow dome, find a snow bridge to cross it, then climb the center of a roughly 40° headwall, staying left of but close to prominent rock outcrops, to the crater rim.

Dirty jugs and white-stained rock; unlike the 5.10 to the left, this route's bolts are in noticeably better shape. Note: published descriptions reportedly mis-locate this route further right than its actual position.
Short scramble up to a belay area, then a brief but engaging climb; the crux is moving up onto a ledge right before the anchor, with a view toward Mt. Rainier in the distance.

moves.value: Just past the first set of bolts on the adjacent route Enchanting Puller Blind (5.10c)
moves.from: Located just past the first set of bolts belonging to the adjacent route Enchanting Puller Blind (5.10c).

beta_new: A sinuous line up the upper wall with bolted belays throughout; rock quality varies, with the crux 4th pitch offering the best stone on the route.

The route's crux is a technical 5.10+ third pitch on comparatively good rock, followed by a harder and more dangerous fourth-pitch 'true crux' — an expanding, sandy crack with poor protection and disintegrating holds (5.10 R). A roughly 20-foot runout section over extremely rotten rock earned the nickname 'the Pitch of Terror.' Bands of loose, decomposing 'kitty litter' rock alternate with sections of solid granite throughout the face.

A moderate, multi-pitch line following the arête on the mountain's northeast side. The rock looks classic but climbs 'shaky,' with numerous fragile flakes of dubious stability and protection that is sometimes insecure.

The standard and by far most-climbed route on Golden Horn. From camp at Snowy Lakes, climbers ascend loose scree and talus on the mountain's southwest side to the summit ridge, then negotiate a short, exposed low-5th-class step — commonly described as a stem or mantle across a gap — to reach the small summit block. Many parties belay or protect the final move with a short rope despite its brevity, given the exposure below.

From high camp, ascend to the saddle/notch and climb the steep, loose gully of the Southwest Couloir (class 4 at the top); a line of more solid darker rock on the left ('the black stairs') offers easier scrambling than the center of the gully.

A long, view-packed off-trail ridge walk rather than a technical climb. Hikers gain the ridge via the steep, unswitchbacked Baldy Trail, cross Baldy's summit (6,827 ft), descend roughly 600 ft to a saddle, cross an intermediate bump, then follow open tundra and talus along the ridge crest to a short Class 2-3 scramble up loose rock to Gray Wolf Ridge's true summit.

From a camp in upper Phelps Basin, climb scree/talus below Dumbell's south side to a 7,900 ft notch on Dumbell's southeast ridge (the final 100 ft to the notch is loose Class 2+), where a long, narrow, airy ledge wraps around Dumbell's east face to the Dumbell-Greenwood col. From the col, an easy Class 2 talus walk up the West Ridge leads to the summit, which has a summit register (kept in a Boy Scouts of America can on the south summit). The route is unroped scrambling throughout, but the connecting ledge is in places only about a foot wide with steep exposure, passes under a small overhang requiring a crawl in one spot, and can hold snow and require an ice axe/crampons into mid-August.
Climbs the big, blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab. Shares its start with Notta Slab, then breaks left into a wide, chimney-like feature after the 2nd bolt. 16 bolts to chain anchors.

moves.from: ; a 70m rope is needed to lower/toprope the full length, and walkers can also descend from the summit

moves.value: Big blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab
moves.from: Climbs the big, blocky groove between Just Enough and Notta Slab.

beta_new: Serious alpine scramble requiring climbing experience and high mountain skills. Technical crux is an exposed class 3-4 hidden ramp with loose rock and significant exposure. A narrow ledge on north side of summit requires careful foot placement, especially in wet or icy conditions. Multiple search and rescue incidents have occurred on this peak.

moves.from: Follows overgrown logging roads and climbers' trails from Barclay Lake, ascending steeply through forest to boulder field approach.

beta_new: There is no official trail to Gunnshy Peak. From a spur road near the Barclay Lake Trailhead, a faint but generally followable climber's path heads east into the forest and leads most of the way to the summit. Along the way parties cross Barclay Creek (log crossing), climb a steep forested headwall to roughly 3,600 ft, drop into and cross a waterfall/stream gully (dry by late summer, medium-to-large flow possible in winter/spring), work through brush and talus past Point 5,760+ near a saddle around 5,360-5,400 ft below Tailgunner (Peak 5,842') and Wing Peak, then either traverse via the Gunn Lake basin (summer/fall) or bypass a rocky buttress on open slopes (winter/spring) to reach the final Class 2-3 summit scramble. Total round trip is roughly 9 miles with 4,300-5,000+ ft of cumulative elevation gain depending on route-finding and how much of the ridge is regained. The route is non-technical but should not be taken for granted — genuine mountaineering skills (route-finding, brush travel, exposed scrambling) are required.

Traverse all four major summits on north-facing ascents and south-facing descents. Features 18 pitches of mostly new climbing: three pitches of 5.10 crack climbing with one aid point used to escape a dead-end fist crack near North Peak summit. Rappel descent includes free-hanging rappel over moat onto Blue Glacier in darkness.

Scramble ~200 feet of loose, mossy, dirty slabs to reach first anchor. Climb 6 pitches of mixed alpine rock through crumbly terrain to Lunch Ledge at ~300 feet. The iconic traverse (pitches 4-5) traverses right on good ledges with old fixed pitons; now requires careful downclimbing due to 2021 damage. Upper pitches climb Class 4 ramp terrain with trees and exposure to summit. Route is sustained and exposed throughout; not a beginner alpine rock climb.

moves.from: Start from Alpental parking lot and reach the talus cone by a line that avoids the private Strasse roads (no established path).

beta_new: Ascend a very large ramp that traverses the entire face from north to south. The climbing starts up a steep crack/face (crux) for approximately 30 feet of low 5th class, then transitions to Class 4 for about half a rope length through rocks and alpine trees with exposure. Climbing continues via mixed scrambling and rock sections to the summit. Route involves significant high-consequence scrambling.

moves.from: From Alpental parking, make a rising traverse up talus to the far left (north) side of the west face (note private road access restrictions as of 2021).

beta_new: From a large clearing around 4000-4200 ft, climb to the saddle between Cave Ridge and Guye Peak, then turn right (south) and follow the ridge to Guye's north summit — class 3 in summer. The 'Hidden Ridge' variation continues from the north summit around an outcropping to a hidden ridge with one 5.4 move (otherwise class 4), rappelling ~30 ft off a slung horn to the notch between the north and middle summits; this was found to be a more direct, more enjoyable line than the standard gully descent in winter/spring conditions.

moves.from: Park at Alpental near the Snow Lake Trailhead and start up the unsigned Cave Ridge/Snoqualmie Mountain climbers' trail beginning about 100 ft south of the Snow Lake Trail.

beta_new: A Grade II snow climb and the steepest of Guye's gully lines. The angle runs about 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then gets progressively steeper the higher you go, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. It finishes at the ridge separating the true and false summits. About half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which the first-ascent party found gave pretty solid snow under the surface - a useful characteristic that also means conditions can differ markedly between the two halves on a warm day. Protection is minimal: an ice axe is mandatory and crampons are required, a picket and rope are suggested (a 50m is preferred over a 30m), rock protection is scarce in peak season, and slung trees provide occasional belays. This is a route where good snow makes it straightforward and bad snow makes it seriously exposed.

From the Cougar Divide Trailhead (~4,900 ft), the unmaintained Cougar Divide Trail #601 climbs along a ridge crest through meadows and old growth to its high point near 5,920 ft (about 3.1 miles in). From there the route continues cross-country along the open ridge, crossing toward Dobbs Cleaver/Chowder Ridge, to merge with the Skyline Divide approach below Hadley Peak's northwest ridge. The final push to the summit is Class 2 with a brief Class 3 step over loose scree, with generally mild exposure for experienced scramblers.
The last push is Class 2 with a short Class 3 step, climbing loose scree and talus to the summit; exposure is generally minimal for experienced parties.

moves.from: From the Skyline Divide Trailhead, a rugged, eroded trail switchbacks through forest to the ridge crest at about 2 miles, then rolls over a series of knolls along the open crest to the trail's high point (~6,563 ft) at about 4.5 miles.

moves.value: Past the high point the maintained tread fades into a boot-packed path that follows the open ridge crest for roughly another 3 miles, over minor ups and downs on Chowder Ridge, to the base of the final scramble.
moves.from: From there the maintained tread fades into a boot-packed path that continues along the open ridge crest for roughly another 3 miles, crossing minor ups and downs on Chowder Ridge, before reaching the base of Hadley Peak's final scramble.

beta_new: Fully bolted (8 bolts) single-pitch sport route starting from a ledge about 25 feet off the ground; features small intrusions used as footholds/handholds on otherwise blank-looking granite. Low traffic and lightly documented — expect an adventurous, quiet outing.
